content: 1. The ability of healthcare professionals to deliver services was assessed on a scale from 1 to 100 in one observational study. The study was not considered to have serious limitations, but the evidence quality was rated as low. This outcome was deemed critical. 2. The ability of students to deliver services post-training was evaluated using surveys or questionnaires in one randomized trial. The study was not considered to have serious limitations, but the evidence was rated as moderate quality. This outcome was also deemed critical. 3. The ability of students to deliver services six months post-training, during their clerkship, was assessed in one randomized trial with a six-month follow-up using surveys or questionnaires. The study was not considered to have serious limitations, but the evidence was rated as moderate quality. This outcome was deemed critical. 4. Another observational study assessed students' ability to deliver services post-training. The study was not considered to have serious limitations, and the evidence was rated as high quality due to strong associations and plausible residual confounding that would reduce the observed effect. This outcome was deemed critical. 5. Students' satisfaction with the training was assessed using a 100-point visual analog scale (VAS) and questionnaires in two randomized trials. The studies were not considered to have serious limitations, but the evidence was rated as moderate quality. This outcome was deemed critical. 6. A narrative review reported on the ability of healthcare professionals to deliver services in general, but no formal measures were specified. 7. A qualitative study reported on the ability of inpatient rehabilitation clinicians, including physical therapists, occupational therapists, and their assistants, to deliver services to manual wheelchair users. Only physical therapists and their assistants were aware of clinical guidelines or the Wheelchair Skills Training Programme (WSTP). 8. One narrative review reported on disruptions in wheelchair use, including those caused by wheelchair breakdowns. No formal measures were specified. 9. Another narrative review reported on wheelchair abandonment, but no formal measures were specified. 10. Three workshops were conducted to train participants in wheelchair service delivery. These included a multimodal workshop with didactic, practical, community, and reflective elements; an educational wheelchair program with interactive experiences; and wheelchair transfer procedures using scenario simulations. These workshops were found to improve participants' confidence and ability to teach transfer skills, activities of daily living (ADLs), and basic mobility to wheelchair users. 11. Training methods outside of professional qualification programs, such as self-directed learning, job shadowing, workshops, presentations, continued education, and clinical seminars, were found to improve healthcare professionals' confidence and ability to deliver wheelchair services. 12. A pre-post study reported that simulation training using different scenarios improved the ability of service providers to perform complex patient transfers. 13. Another study found that most students agreed their comfort in treating patients increased after training, and their ability to assess, train, spot, and document wheelchair users' skills significantly improved. 14. A cross-sectional study reported on the ability of service providers to deliver services, while a qualitative study explored the same topic among occupational therapy and medical students. 15. Academic rehabilitation programs continue to evolve to ensure wheelchair service provision is included in professional training. 16. Two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) reported on satisfaction with wheelchair services among undergraduate occupational therapy and medical students. A pre-post study also reported on satisfaction among occupational therapy students. 17. A strong recommendation was made for seamless and integrated wheelchair provision across all levels of health systems and relevant sectors. This includes identification of need, referral, and service delivery steps such as selection, fitting, training, and follow-up. The evidence supporting this recommendation was of very low certainty. 18. Seamless wheelchair provision is characterized by consistency, continuity, and coordination of service steps in a timely manner with minimal barriers and delays. Integration means that wheelchair provision is part of comprehensive health services at all levels (primary, secondary, tertiary) and, where appropriate, part of other relevant sectors such as social, vocational, or welfare services. 19. Fragmented or ad hoc systems were found to cause significant harm to wheelchair users by delaying or denying access to wheelchairs, accessories, and necessary service steps. These harms included negative impacts on health, social inclusion, and economic participation. 20. Seamless systems were determined to be feasible in low-, middle-, and high-income countries and were associated with cost savings and reduced financial burdens on wheelchair users. 21. The systematic review identified 20 studies with outcomes rated critical or important for seamless systems. However, the quality of almost all studies was graded as very low, resulting in very low overall certainty of evidence. 22. Members of the guideline development group (GDG) noted that fragmented systems increased financial burdens on wheelchair users and their families, while seamless systems reduced costs and improved service delivery efficiency. 23. Practice-based evidence from GDG members indicated that seamless referral and access systems were feasible and beneficial in all contexts, outweighing any potential harms and justifying the cost of implementation. 24. The GDG emphasized the need for comprehensive long-term economic evaluations to link seamless systems to reduced health expenditures and increased economic productivity for wheelchair users and their caregivers. However, they strongly believed that the benefits of implementation would outweigh the costs. 25. Fragmented systems were found to impose severe harms on wheelchair users, including secondary complications, extreme isolation, restricted participation, and severely impaired mobility and posture. In some cases, these harms could lead to death.
